text: Welcome to Chapter Six of ServiceNow Performance and Troubleshooting. This lesson covers triaging a platform-wide slowdown — what to actually check, and in what order, before you touch anything.

When several users report the instance feels slow, that is a claim, not a confirmed fact. Users experience the platform through whatever they personally touch — their incident queue, their catalog item, their dashboard. If the one area they all happen to use is degraded, it feels universal to every one of them, even if nothing else on the platform is affected at all. A real platform-wide slowdown and a loud, widely-used feature that's degraded are two different incidents, requiring two different responses, and they produce the exact same first report: it's slow. Triage exists to tell them apart before committing to a fix for either one.

Triage runs in three ordered steps. First, confirm scope with the Instance Health Dashboard from Chapter Four — does it show response time, volume, and error rate moving together across the whole instance, or is this really one loud feature mistaken for a platform event? Second, if scope is confirmed, check the deployment timeline: a change that runs on every transaction, like a new Business Rule on a heavily-used table, is the most common real cause of a sudden, platform-wide slowdown. Third, if there's no deployment correlation, check semaphore and node usage for resource exhaustion — a runaway scheduled job or genuine capacity pressure produces the same instance-wide symptom but needs a completely different fix.

A bad deployment, a runaway job, and genuine capacity pressure all look identical from a user's chair — each one starts with the same user complaint, on the same symptom. But each one needs a completely different response: rolling back a release, killing or rescheduling a job, or addressing genuine infrastructure capacity. That's exactly why gathering evidence through all three steps, in order, has to come before attempting any fix at all.
Next up: when a triaged issue actually needs ServiceNow's own support team, and what evidence makes that conversation go well.
